## The prize went to the people who kept the thing running

The [2026 Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2026-07-22-oxford-university-statistician-co-awarded-prestigious-1-million-rousseeuw-prize) has gone to five people for building and maintaining R: [Brian Ripley](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/), Martin Maechler, Kurt Hornik, Peter Dalgaard, and Luke Tierney. Prizes in statistics usually reward a theorem or a method. This one rewards a piece of software that several million people rely on and almost nobody thinks about — which is the harder thing to get recognised, and the reason it is worth marking.

Professor Ripley's share of that work is understood to be enormous. Over the decades he is reckoned to have personally written the large majority of base R's codebase — the exact accounting is not something anyone has published a number for, but the direction of it is not in dispute among people who have watched the project. That is what a prize like this is really for.

## We got the broken builds first

I was Professor Ripley's doctoral student in the R 0.7 era, working on high-dimensional ordinal classification with an SVM-related algorithm. What I remember most is not a seminar. It is that he would hand his students pre-release builds of R and expect us to go and use them on our actual work before anyone else saw them.

There was nothing formal about it. No tracker, no test plan, no word like "QA". A graduate student with a real dataset and a deadline is a very effective way of finding out what breaks, and he had several of us. We were an early bug-testing team who mostly did not realise that was the arrangement.

## The mailing list met a different man

That is not how the wider R world knew him. On the mailing lists he was blunt to the point of legend, terse in a way that has been [affectionately documented](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2013/06/ripley-facts/) ever since. Community lore also held that he answered posts at every hour of the day and night — I have no way to verify the sleep schedule, and the running joke that he never slept was always more affectionate than literal. But the joke only worked because the volume was real: an extraordinary amount of unpaid time spent answering strangers' questions about their code.

## What the prize is actually honouring

As a supervisor, Professor Ripley was patient, and generous with insight — a few well-placed sentences that reorganised a month of work. None of that came through in three-line mailing-list replies, and it did not need to. The prize honours decades of unglamorous infrastructure work, done mostly out of sight, that a great deal of statistics now quietly runs on.
